blocks.content: 1. INTRODUCTION TO MODAL VERBS

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Modal verbs are auxiliary verbs used to express ability, permission, possibility, necessity, or obligation.
Modals are always followed by the base form of the verb (V1) and do not take -s, -ed, or -ing suffixes.
Need and Dare function as marginal/semi-modals, acting as both main verbs and auxiliary verbs.
Modal Perfect constructions (e.g., should have + V3) express past unfulfilled actions, regrets, or past logical deductions.
Ought to and Should convey advice or moral duty, whereas Must implies strong compulsion or legal obligation.

blocks.content:
Modal verbs are special helping verbs used to express ability, permission, possibility, obligation, advice, necessity, and probability.



Unlike main verbs, modal verbs do not change their form according to tense or subject. They are always followed by the base form of the verb (V1).



Modal verbs are extremely important for SSC examinations because they are frequently tested in Error Detection, Fill in the Blanks, Sentence Improvement, and Cloze Tests.



Example:

• She can swim.

• You must follow the rules.



Golden Principle:

Modal + V1 (always)
2. CHARACTERISTICS OF MODAL VERBS

1. Modals do not take ‘s’, ‘es’, ‘ing’, or ‘ed’ forms.

Incorrect: He cans swim.

Correct: He can swim.



2. Modals are followed directly by the base verb.

Incorrect: She can to sing.

Correct: She can sing.



3. Two modals cannot be used together.

Incorrect: He will can go.

Correct: He will be able to go.
3. LIST OF COMMON MODALS
Can, Could, May, Might, Shall, Should, Will, Would, Must, Ought to, Need, Dare.
4. CAN

Uses of CAN:



1. Ability:

She can solve difficult problems.



2. Informal Permission:

Can I leave early today?



3. Possibility:

Anyone can make mistakes.



SSC Trap:

Incorrect: I cannot be able to do this.

Correct: I cannot do this.

Correct: I will not be able to do this.
5. COULD

Uses of COULD:



1. Past Ability:

He could run very fast in his childhood.



2. Polite Request:

Could you help me with this file?



3. Weak Possibility:

It could rain tonight.



Difference Between CAN and COULD:

‘Could’ is more polite and less certain than ‘can’.
6. MAY

Uses of MAY:



1. Formal Permission:

May I come in?



2. Strong Possibility:

The results may be announced tomorrow.



3. Wishes:

May you live long.



SSC Trap:

Avoid using ‘possibly’ with may.



Incorrect: He may possibly come.

Correct: He may come.
7. MIGHT

Uses of MIGHT:



1. Very Weak Possibility:

She might miss the train.



2. Past Possibility:

He might have forgotten the meeting.



Key Difference:

May → higher probability

Might → lower probability
8. SHALL

Uses of SHALL:



1. Suggestions:

Shall we start the meeting?



2. Offers:

Shall I help you?



3. Formal Orders:

You shall obey the rules.



Modern Note:

In contemporary English, ‘will’ is more commonly used than ‘shall’.
9. WILL

Uses of WILL:



1. Future Actions:

I will call you tomorrow.



2. Determination:

I will succeed.



3. Promises:

I will always support you.
10. WOULD

Uses of WOULD:



1. Polite Requests:

Would you open the window?



2. Past Habit:

When we were children, we would play outside.



3. Imaginary Situations:

If I were rich, I would travel the world.
11. SHOULD

Uses of SHOULD:



1. Advice:

You should revise daily.



2. Duty:

We should respect our teachers.



3. Expectation:

The train should arrive on time.

rows: 'Can you swim?' (Ability) vs. 'May I come in?' (Permission)
Strong Compulsion / Rule (Must) vs. Advice / Recommendation (Should)
'You must follow traffic rules.' vs. 'You should revise daily.'
Auxiliary: 'He dare not speak.' / Main Verb: 'He does not dare to speak.'

blocks.content: 12. MUST

Uses of MUST:



1. Strong Obligation:

You must wear a helmet.



2. Logical Deduction:

The lights are off; they must be sleeping.



3. Rules:

Candidates must carry identification proof.
13. OUGHT TO

Uses of OUGHT TO:



1. Moral Duty:

We ought to help the poor.



2. Strong Advice:

You ought to apologize.
14. NEED

Need can function both as a modal and a main verb.



As a Modal:

You need not worry.



As a Main Verb:

You need to work hard.



Rule:

When used as a modal in negative sentences, ‘to’ is not used.
15. DARE

Dare is used to express courage and can act as both a modal and a main verb.



As a Modal:

He dare not challenge me.



As a Main Verb:

He dared to speak the truth.
16. MODAL PERFECT (VERY IMPORTANT FOR SSC)

Modal Perfect is formed using:



Modal + have + V3



It refers to past possibilities, regrets, or assumptions.



Examples:



• He must have forgotten the keys. (Strong assumption)

• She could have won the race. (Ability but not done)

• You should have studied harder. (Regret/advice)

• They might have taken the wrong route. (Possibility)
17. HIGH-PROBABILITY SSC RULES

items: Common Error: Modals must be followed by base verb V1 (e.g., 'He can solves' is wrong; correct is 'He can solve').
Semi-modals ('Need' and 'Dare') do not take 'to' when used as auxiliary modals in negative or interrogative sentences (e.g., 'You need not go', not 'You need not to go').
'Should have + V3' denotes an action that was expected to happen in the past but did not occur.
Do not use two modals together in a single clause (e.g., 'He should can do it' is incorrect).

blocks.content:
1. Modal is always followed by V1.

2. Never use two modals together.

3. Do not use ‘to’ after modal verbs (except ‘ought to’).

4. Use ‘have + V3’ to refer to past situations.

5. ‘Need not’ means absence of necessity.
18. COMMON ERRORS IN EXAMINATIONS

Incorrect: He can sings very well.

Correct: He can sing very well.



Incorrect: You must to follow the rules.

Correct: You must follow the rules.



Incorrect: She will can solve the problem.

Correct: She will be able to solve the problem.
19. PRACTICE QUESTIONS (SSC LEVEL)

Error Detection:



1. She can dances very well.

2. You must to complete the work.

3. He could not able to solve the puzzle.



Fill in the blanks:



1. You ______ obey the traffic rules. (must/should)

2. ______ you help me with this task? (would/shall)

3. She ______ have missed the train. (may/must)



Answers:

1. dance

2. remove 'to'

3. able error

Fill blanks → must, would, may.
20. CHAPTER SUMMARY

Modal verbs improve sentence clarity by expressing attitude, certainty, and obligation.



Key Takeaways:



• Modal + V1 is the golden rule.

• Use modal perfect for past assumptions.

• Avoid double modals.

• Remember the difference between ‘may’ and ‘might’.

• Use ‘should’ for advice and ‘must’ for obligation.



Mastery of modals greatly improves accuracy in SSC grammar questions.
